item.title: Lab 1.3: From Templates to Features — What One Hidden Layer Does to the Weights
item.description:
Lab 1.3: From Templates to Features — What One Hidden Layer Does to the Weights

MNIST internals series. Lab 1.1 gave us the clean answer: in a linear softmax model, a weight row is a matched-filter photograph of its class. Lab 1.2 showed those photographs being painted, re-carved, and out-bid.

Now the question this series was really building toward: add one hidden layer. What happens to the weight picture?

If you’ve watched 3Blue1Brown’s neural nets series, you might expect: “layers learn edges, then curves, then parts; visualizing raw weights won’t tell you much here.” We can now test that ourselves instead of taking it on faith, and the truth lands in a more interesting place:

item.title: Lab 2.1: How Word Vectors Learn to Mean — Embeddings From Zero, and What They Secretly Compute
item.description:
Lab 2.1: How Word Vectors Learn to Mean — Embeddings From Zero, and What They Secretly Compute

Language-model internals series. In the MNIST series we took apart what weights represent for vision. New series, same ritual — build it from scratch, check gradients numerically, claim nothing without a baseline or a measured number.

The question for this lab, in the plainest possible form:

A word becomes a row of numbers. How can those numbers possibly mean anything?

item.title: Lab 1.1: MNIST From Pixels to a Neural Network — What Do the Weights Actually Represent?
item.description:
Lab 1.1: What Do the Weights of a Neural Network Actually Represent?

MNIST internals series — the practical companion to the ML notes (softmax & cross-entropy, backprop, training a 2-layer network). This time we stop deriving and start looking.

Anyone who has trained a model eventually asks:

The model is just a pile of numbers. In this lab’s case, exactly 7,860 of them (7,850 weights + 10 biases). What do those numbers actually mean?

item.title: Training a 2-Layer Network in NumPy: From Scalar to Vectorized Backprop
item.description:
Training a 2-Layer Network in NumPy: From Scalar to Vectorized Backprop

The previous note did the backward pass for a small 2-layer network by hand, one scalar at a time. That is the best way to understand what backprop actually does.

This note takes the next step: turn that scalar walk into compact, vectorized NumPy code. The math is unchanged; the only thing that changes is notation. I will introduce every matrix slowly — what its rows and columns mean, where the division by the batch size comes from, and why it is exactly the same algorithm you already did by hand.

item.title: ML Refresher: Linear and Logistic Regression
item.description:
ML Refresher: Linear and Logistic Regression

This is the first note in the ML → Deep Learning → Transformers → LLMs series. The goal is to rebuild working memory of the basics before we get to neural networks: what a model is, how a loss function measures error, and how gradient descent tunes parameters.

We will implement linear regression and logistic regression from scratch in NumPy, then compare with scikit-learn. If the code and gradients feel obvious, you are ready for the next note (computational graphs and backprop). If not, this is exactly the foundation to lock down first.
